clue.text: Round head of moor is jolly high

indicators.note: the jolly word goes round the outside of the moor's first letter, so Round signals a container

parts.note: jolly means gay in its old sense of merry

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here taken from moor

explanation.surface: Someone cheerfully remarks that a rounded hilltop on the moor is splendidly lofty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' puts GAY around M, the head of 'moor'. 'High' here is said of game meat that has hung until strong-smelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat or game that is gamy has been hung until strong and pungent, which is what high means of meat.

clue.text: Try to rise twice, and fall

parts.note: to have a go is to try
a down is a rolling hill, a rise of ground
a hill is a rise of ground

explanation.surface: Advice to keep attempting to stand up even after tumbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise' is used twice as a noun: DOWN (as in the South Downs, chalk hills) and HILL.
explanation.definitionFit: To go downhill is to decline or deteriorate, which matches fall in the sense of a drop.

clue.text: One warming hands, old ears (alternately)- and neck

definitions.text: One warming hands, old ears (alternately)- and neck

parts.note: a muff is a fur tube that keeps the hands warm

indicators.note: alternately picks every other letter of old ears, starting from the second

explanation.surface: A list of winter wear: something for the hands, the ears and the neck.
explanation.walkthrough: '(alternately)' gives L, E, R from 'old ears'. The whole clue doubles as a description of a scarf.
explanation.definitionFit: A muffler is a warm scarf wound round the neck, akin to the muff that keeps hands warm.

clue.text: Back crazy request to girl for source of attar

indicators.note: Back tells us to read the word for crazy from right to left

parts.note: crazy means mad
to request is to ask
Rose is a girl's name

explanation.surface: An instruction to return a madcap request to a young woman, in search of perfume oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns MAD into DAM. Attar is a perfume oil distilled from rose petals.
explanation.definitionFit: Attar of roses is pressed mainly from the damask rose, a fragrant old variety, so it is the oil's source.

clue.text: The exact opposite, as pointed out

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of as pointed are put out of order

explanation.surface: Someone claims something is the very reverse, as indicated.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipodes means a direct opposite, from places on diametrically opposite sides of the globe.

clue.text: Advantage of hound not evident at first

indicators.note: not evident at first means the hound's opening letter is missing

parts.note: a basset is a short-legged hunting hound

explanation.surface: The benefit of keeping a dog is not obvious at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not evident at first' removes B from BASSET.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is a useful quality or resource, something that gives an advantage.

clue.text: A Life of the Marches is very dark, lit badly

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters of is very dark lit are put in a disordered arrangement

explanation.surface: A biography of the Welsh border country is gloomy and poorly lit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges IS VERY DARK LIT. The Marches are the borderlands between England and Wales, where the Reverend Francis Kilvert lived and wrote.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian curate Francis Kilvert's journal records daily life in the Welsh border country, the Marches.

clue.text: Book the First, for One

definitions.meaning: a church service book setting out the rites for ordaining clergy
a number showing position such as first, as against the counting number one

explanation.walkthrough: Capitals disguise 'First' and 'One' as titles; first is the positional form of the counting number one.
explanation.definitionFit: First is an ordinal number, the order-giving partner of the cardinal one; the word also names a church service book.

clue.text: Seabird sailors shot through middle of feet

indicators.note: shot through means one piece runs right through the other, so the sailors go inside
middle of takes the central letters of feet

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy, sailors

explanation.surface: A seabird is hit by sailors' shot through its webbed feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot through' poses as gunfire at the bird but is the container signal; 'middle of' takes the two central letters of 'feet'.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed sea eagle, a large seabird of coasts.

clue.text: There's something lacking if edict has to be put out

indicators.note: put out means disturbed or disordered, so the letters of if edict are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that a decree is missing something if it has to be published.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be put out' rearranges IF EDICT; 'put out' poses as issuing a decree.
explanation.definitionFit: A deficit is a shortfall, an amount by which something falls short or is lacking.

clue.text: Sort of TV of course that's not working

parts.note: a closed shop or factory is not working
a circuit is a course, as in a racing circuit

explanation.surface: A television set has naturally stopped functioning.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in reverse order in the clue; 'of course' looks like 'naturally'.
explanation.definitionFit: Closed-circuit television is a camera system relayed to a limited set of screens, a kind of TV.

clue.text: Richard's opponent's condition after light lunch?

definitions.text: Richard's opponent's condition after light lunch?

parts.words: Richard's opponent's condition after light lunch?
parts.note: Richard the Lionheart's Saracen foe on the Crusades, read jokingly as the state of having a light green meal inside you

explanation.walkthrough: Split as SALAD IN, the name describes someone who has just eaten a salad. Richard is Richard I of England, the crusader king.
explanation.definitionFit: The Muslim sultan who opposed Richard I in the Third Crusade bore this name, which splits into a meal plus a word for inside.

clue.text: Markings on bat from China?

parts.note: a cricket bat is made of willow, so its grain might be thought of as markings; the phrase is really a famous blue design on Chinese-style plates

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket bats are made from willow wood, which is the joke; 'China' is really china, crockery.
explanation.definitionFit: The blue-and-white design of bridge, birds and trees painted on china plates carries this name, and willow is also bat timber.

clue.text: Committal having alien finally confined

indicators.note: confined means the final letter of alien is held within the word for committal

parts.note: committal of a body is its burial, interment

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of alien

explanation.surface: A person committed to custody because the foreigner was finally locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confined' puts N, the last of 'alien', into INTERMENT. The whole clue also describes holding enemy aliens in wartime.
explanation.definitionFit: Internment is the confinement of enemy aliens or suspects without trial, a committal to detention.

clue.text: Host makes way into garden

indicators.note: into signals that the abbreviation for way is placed inside the gardening word

parts.note: to garden is to hoe
Rd is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: A party host clears a path into the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Host' looks like a party-giver but means a multitude.
explanation.definitionFit: A host is a great number of people, and so is a horde: the two are synonyms for a crowd.

clue.text: Event in Irish town unfinished after a month

indicators.note: after places the shortened town second, following the month

parts.note: Dec is the abbreviation for December

indicators.note: unfinished means the town's name loses its last letter

parts.note: Athlone is a town in the Irish midlands

explanation.surface: Something happened in an Irish town that was left incomplete a month later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' cuts ATHLONE to ATHLON. 'Event' is an athletics event.
explanation.definitionFit: The decathlon is a single athletics event made of ten disciplines.

clue.text: Round stone is to produce rattle

indicators.note: Round means the word for produce goes around the stone

parts.note: to produce is to create
a pit is the stone of a fruit

explanation.surface: Advice on making a noise by putting a pebble in a container.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round stone' looks like a pebble, but 'Round' is the container signal and 'stone' is a fruit's pit; 'is to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: To crepitate is to make a crackling or rattling sound, as in medicine of lungs.

clue.text: Fail in court to secure title at first, so decline socially

indicators.note: to secure means to hold fast, so the phrase for failing in court encloses the letter

parts.note: to fail in court is to lose a case

indicators.note: at first takes only the opening letter of title

explanation.surface: A litigant fails to win a title deed and slides down the social ladder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to secure' puts T, title at first, inside LOSE CASE.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose caste is to fall in social rank, drop to a lower standing in society.

clue.text: Said more than enough for fine, being tried

indicators.note: for signals one piece standing in place of another within said

parts.note: A1 means first-rate or fine, written as AI
ample means more than enough

explanation.surface: Someone said too much in exchange for a fine and was put on trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' swaps AI (A1, first-rate) in SAID for AMPLE. 'Fine' and 'tried' pose as courtroom words.
explanation.definitionFit: To have sampled something is to have tried it, tested a little of it.

clue.text: Boy wearing cap and cape lying in the sand

indicators.note: lying in means the abbreviation for cape sits inside the word for sand

parts.note: a dune is a ridge of sand
C is the map abbreviation for cape

explanation.surface: A child in hat and cloak lies on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lying in' puts C inside DUNE. The cap is the pointed dunce's cap once put on slow pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow pupil was once made to wear a conical paper hat, the dunce's cap, so the boy in it is the dullard.

clue.text: Capital Spaniard raised, expending energy for nothing

indicators.note: expending means giving up one letter in exchange for another
raised in a down clue means the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: an Iberian is a native of the peninsula holding Spain
E is the physics symbol for energy
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A Spanish worker in a capital is promoted after spending energy for no reward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns IBERIAN into NAIREBI; 'expending' trades its E for O.
explanation.definitionFit: Nairobi is the capital city of Kenya.

clue.text: Married, keep losing head — shame!

indicators.note: losing head means the word for keep drops its first letter

parts.note: a keep is a castle stronghold, a fortification

explanation.surface: A married man ashamed at losing his authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing head' cuts FORTIFICATION to ORTIFICATION. 'Keep' is the noun, a castle tower, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Mortification is the feeling of deep embarrassment and humiliation, a synonym of shame.

clue.text: Cooler at height, so get coat

parts.note: ice is a cooler, something that chills
up means at height, aloft

explanation.surface: It's colder up high, so put on a jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coat' here is a coating of ice, not a jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: To ice up is to become covered in a layer of ice, to get a frozen coating.

clue.text: Weapon locked up by keeper

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the hidden letters are read bottom to top
locked means the letters are held within the word keeper

explanation.surface: A weapon is put away by the custodian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'locked' finds EEPE in 'keeper'; 'up' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: An épée is a fencing sword, a weapon.

clue.text: Add impurities to cement after cut-back

indicators.note: after places the cement word second, following the reversed cut
back means the word for cut is read in reverse

parts.note: to lop is to cut
lute is a clay or cement used to seal joints

explanation.surface: A builder adds cement after a cut-back in a project, compromising its quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LOP into POL. LUTE is a sealing paste of clay or cement.
explanation.definitionFit: To pollute is to contaminate, making something impure by adding harmful substances.

clue.text: Further bird that talks back to golden eagles' leader

indicators.note: back means the talking bird's name is read in reverse

parts.note: the myna is a bird that mimics speech
or is gold in heraldry

indicators.note: leader takes the first letter of eagles'

explanation.surface: An aviary keeper sends a talking bird back to the head of the golden eagles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns MYNA into ANYM. OR is the heraldic word for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Any more means further or additionally, as in 'not wanting any more'.

clue.text: Finishes, having surpassed such a line —- no sense going on

definitions.text: such a line —- no sense going on

parts.note: finishes, as a noun, means ends
to surpass is to top

explanation.surface: A poet finishes after outdoing a line whose meaning does not continue.
explanation.walkthrough: In verse, a line whose sense finishes at its end without running into the next is the opposite of enjambed.
explanation.definitionFit: An end-stopped line of poetry has a pause at the line's close because its meaning is complete there, not carried over.

clue.text: Scotsman chosen to speak

indicators.note: to speak signals that the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: chosen means picked

explanation.surface: A Scot is selected to give a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The Picts were an ancient people of northern Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pict was one of the early inhabitants of Scotland, so a Scotsman of old.
